Registration remains available for its validity plus a bounded historical-verification window; revocation high-water marks outlive removed certificates. The full acceptance-time evidence is forwarded inside the encrypted mail bundle. Delete expired challenges and failed upload bodies. Do not include report spools in routine backups by default. Limit logs to aggregate health/error classes; review observability settings for token/signature leakage.

V1 has no padding bytes: its exact framing ends at EOF after the attachment. A future version may define authenticated padding to policy-defined size buckets inside client encryption, with explicit framing and interoperability fixtures; overhead counts toward quotas. Batching/delay is optional and disabled for urgent incident reports by default. Static age keys do not supply forward secrecy; rotation and short retention reduce exposure but do not erase mail archives. Supported post-quantum encryption can address future cryptanalysis, not private-key theft. True forward secrecy needs a separately reviewed protocol/key lifecycle.

Nineteen original findings grouped into ten controls#

Review itemR-numberOwning mechanismRequired acceptance requirements
1. Proper-encryption claimR01Opaque admission; maintainer full decryptionSigned malformed ciphertext cannot be labeled encryption-verified; recipient rejects it
2. Circular recipient trustR02Independent threshold-dual-authorized policy, pinning, on-chain sequence/currentnessSubstituted recipient, withheld on-chain update and rolled-back policy rejected before local encryption
3. Unsafe reuse of make relayR00Public registration only; separate confidential transport/sign-only adapterNo report contents enter Discord workflow; original evidence or labeled registrar attestations required
4. Powerful key exposureR04, R18Ed25519 delegation and scoped renewal/revocationRoutine reports work without node keyring access; delegate cannot extend its own authority
5. Signature binding/replay/authorshipR05, R06, R07Inner content signature, outer context/ciphertext signature, durable atomic outboxChanged destination/file/context rejected; retries/concurrency/restarts produce one accepted job
6. Valid operator definitionR03, R08Exact account authority, fresh state, explicit statuses/recoveryUnrelated provider/self-generated signer rejected; Standby incident reporting succeeds
7. Tor and identity limitsR09, R16, R17SOCKS-only transport, pinned onion, honest privacy promiseProxy failure/redirect cannot produce direct egress; relay identity visibility documented
8. Whole-report/email privacyR10, R11Client package encryption, encrypted forwarding bundle, generic mail, retentionMail provider cannot see node identity/message/filename; static-key exposure remains explicit
9. Abuse/hostile attachmentsR13, R14Admission-before-body, quotas/caps, staged recipient verificationSlow/large/authorized floods bounded; no unsafe opening/extraction or partial output presentation
10. Delivery/test separationR12, R15Durable status, maintainer-signed ack, distinct policy/keys/routesSMTP acceptance differs from acknowledgement; startup rejects cross-environment configuration, keys and routes

Also test registration key possession, public-announcement substitution, compromised Discord/registrar behavior, wrong maintainer role, simultaneous epoch rotations, emergency freeze persistence, capability substitution, storage loss/restart, retention cleanup, and post-compromise receipt backdating limits. Independent protocol review and implementation evidence are required before marking any control implemented.

Evolution into secure operator and trusted-group communications#

The intended direction includes operator-to-operator conversations and conversations with THORNode developers and explicitly trusted groups. V1 implements confidential reporting and bounded encrypted replies only. The identity registry is a foundation for later messaging; a report registration is not a grant to join any group, discover all operators, or retrieve another operator's inbox.

Reuse a messaging system; own identity and authorization#

Bodferd should own the chain-to-communication identity binding, developer-role attestations, verification display and group admission policy. It should delegate conversation encryption, session state and device management to an established system or independently reviewed implementation. Evaluate an integration with an existing end-to-end encrypted messenger before building a separate transport. Signal documents distinct protocols for key agreement, ratcheting and multi-device sessions; importing its library alone does not establish compatibility with the Signal service. Signal technical documentation.

The owner selected MLS as the lead investigation candidate, retaining libsignal as an alternative. Evaluate maintained implementations of Messaging Layer Security; an independent audit of the selected version/integration remains required before production and must not be assumed from RFC conformance. RFC 9420 specifies asynchronous group key establishment with forward secrecy and post-compromise security. MLS is a cryptographic component, not a complete chat application, identity directory or anonymity system. Selection of a product/library, versions and license compatibility remains a separate design decision. RFC 9420.

Do not turn the email relay into a chat server, distribute a shared static age group identity, build a home-grown ratchet, or treat adding recipients to an age header as group membership security. V1 report keys and durable content signatures retain their original semantics. Separate protocol versions and keys must distinguish future conversation traffic from evidentiary incident reports; conversation authentication and deniability requirements need explicit review rather than automatically signing every chat message with the report key.

Identity and group boundaries#

PrincipalAuthority sourceWhat it can authorize
Node parent authorityCurrent exact chain relationship and supported parent evidenceScoped member grants; cannot appoint maintainers or grant membership in arbitrary groups
Authorized team memberCurrent parent-authorized member credential and explicit capabilitiesIts own communication/device identity; requested group enrollment, subject to separate group policy
THORNode developer / maintainerIndependent signed role roster, with out-of-band bootstrapActions allowed by that developer role; no automatic node account authority
Group administratorExplicit group-specific policyInvitations, removals and permitted membership changes in that group
Directory / delivery serverNo independent role-granting authorityRouting and bounded storage; no silent key substitution or membership expansion
Optional zkgroup authentication issuerPolicy-authorized custody of ServerSecretParams; a trusted issuance authorityCan mint supported UID authentication credentials; sees issuance identities, and compromise permits forged issuance; not merely a ciphertext router

Future device credentials bind a device's messaging-protocol public keys to its scoped member ID, parent scope, communication identity, environment, expiry, credential sequence and allowed purposes. A node may have several people and each person several devices; neither a node ID nor a shared team alias authorizes all of them. Member removal revokes that member’s node-derived grants/devices, while independently issued unrelated roles follow their own issuer policy. They use protocol-native keys and formats where required; the age reply key is never silently repurposed. New-device enrollment requires existing trusted-device approval or explicit parent/role-authorized recovery. Merely authenticating to the relay, controlling an email address or presenting a stale node certificate cannot enroll a device. Key changes appear to peers and administrators with a verification path independent of the directory.

Groups have an immutable group identifier, named policy owner, explicit administrator authority, admission assurance, membership visibility and history policy. A node certificate proves eligibility for a policy check, not that its holder is a developer or already belongs to every operator group. Invitations are bounded, single-use and confirmed by the invitee. Parent chain authority is rechecked at relevant membership changes; node exit, role expiry, device compromise and emergency freeze trigger removal of affected devices and protocol-native epoch/key updates. Removed devices cannot decrypt future messages after an applied removal; they retain previously learned plaintext and keys. No remote deletion promise can undo that exposure.

A membership authority cannot silently grant itself all groups. Clients authenticate membership changes against group policy and surface them to members. Directory proofs, detectable equivocation, administrator collusion and roster compromise require evaluation in the selected messaging system; a signed central roster alone does not prevent different clients receiving conflicting authorized views.

Delivery, privacy and recovery requirements#

An optional encrypted mailbox uses per-device opaque delivery capabilities, bounded offline storage and independent quotas. Device-list refresh, key-package/prekey fetches, delivery, receipts, attachments and any push mechanism all need an explicit Tor transport design. Reusing a messenger that contacts its clearnet servers directly would violate Bodferd's intended network boundary; Tor support, DNS behavior and background traffic must be demonstrated, not assumed. Notification previews contain no message text or node identity by default.

Public node enrollment already reveals participation. Group membership, contact graphs, traffic timing, size and device activity may reveal more. V1 does not promise to hide those from its identity-aware relay. A future metadata-hiding delivery service would need a separately reviewed separation between authenticated enrollment and delivery, with abuse controls that do not recreate a global public contact graph. Contact discovery is opt-in and scoped; do not expose a list of all registered operators or arbitrary unauthenticated key lookups.

Forward secrecy depends on endpoint key deletion and implementation behavior, including backups. Backing up ratchet or group secrets may undermine it. Recovery must reestablish device authorization and notify peers; an operator losing all devices cannot transparently regain old conversation history through a server-held decryption master key. History sharing with new members is disabled by default and requires an explicit, visible group decision if supported. Endpoint compromise, a legitimate member copying messages, message truth and censorship remain outside transport encryption's guarantees.

Evidence required before expanding scope#

Before choosing a conversation stack, demonstrate a two-operator and developer-group pilot over Tor; authenticated device replacement; stale-role and removed-device rejection; independent key verification under directory substitution; offline catch-up and conflicting membership-change recovery; bounded malicious-member uploads; and measured metadata exposure. Use the selected protocol's interoperability and security tests and obtain independent review of the identity integration. No production chat or group API is authorized by the v1 report certificate. The decision gate is whether an existing product can meet these requirements with a small identity adapter; if it cannot, record the specific unmet requirements and implementation cost before proposing a new messenger.

MLS-first conversation investigation#

This is the owner-selected investigation order, not approval to implement a messenger. RFC 9420 supplies group establishment, authenticated membership commits, epochs, forward secrecy and post-compromise security under its assumptions. Bodferd supplies the Authentication Service contract: independently verified parent/developer roles, scoped team-member/device credentials and group-specific admission decisions. A separate MLS identity/credential belongs to each admitted person/device; the operator’s node is an eligibility relationship, not a shared group cryptographic identity. A separate largely untrusted Delivery Service stores/routes ciphertext and key packages; it does not grant roles or hold group secrets. RFC 9420.

LayerReused component / Bodferd responsibilityTrust and privacy boundary
Authentication ServiceBodferd credential validation and chain/role evidence; selected MLS credential-validation hookTrusted to bind identities/roles; enrollment observes node-to-device associations; compromise can issue false credentials
MLS endpointUpstream key-package, group commit, epoch and secret managementDevice-local secrets; peers authenticate credentials and group policy before accepting additions/changes
Delivery ServiceTor-only queues, bounded key-package availability and offline deliveryCan suppress/reorder/drop traffic, observe routing/timing/size and potentially group IDs/epochs; no plaintext guarantee against compromised endpoints
Group policy ownerExplicit member/device/administrator authorizationCan approve membership within the group; is not automatically a maintainer or authority for other groups

MLS does not by itself decide whether a node deserves membership. Clients validate the authenticated credential and group-specific policy on every membership change, then apply the protocol-native commit. Role expiry/removal blocks new sends until the removal commit and new epoch are applied; delivery of delayed old-epoch ciphertext does not restore eligibility. A malicious delivery service can withhold commits and split views, so the pilot must demonstrate conflict detection, offline catch-up and convergence without sending new secrets to stale or removed devices. Do not promise removal erases old history or secret material already copied by members.

Candidate libraries are mls-rs (MIT/Apache-2.0) and OpenMLS (MIT); pin actual versions and crypto providers only after tests. mls-rs explicitly states that a full third-party security audit is not yet completed; conformance is not an audit. OpenMLS published a secret-tree persistence advisory GHSA-qr9h-x63w-vqfm, fixed in 0.7.1. These primary sources were checked on 2026-10-14; do not infer audit coverage of Bodferd from a fixed vulnerability. Obtain and review actual audit scope for the chosen release/provider or commission the missing review before production.

Use a supported Rust consumer for the first bounded investigation, or a demonstrably supported upstream binding for the actual target client. Existing UniFFI modules are not evidence of a maintained Go wrapper; no bespoke FFI is authorized. The reporting CLI can remain Go without owning conversation state. Investigate the real credential-validation entry point, key-package lifecycle, storage transactions and interoperability vectors from the selected crate/version rather than write group crypto or a parallel ratchet. Native age report encryption stays separate; no MLS export key silently becomes a report or node signing key.

Acceptance evidence must cover two operators plus a developer group over Tor, per-device authorization, malicious/stale credential rejection, concurrent commits, device recovery, removal during offline/queued traffic, state rollback/crash handling, storage-key deletion/backups and measured exposed metadata. All key-package fetches, ciphertext delivery, attachment storage and notifications must follow the Tor boundary. No APNs/FCM or other clearnet background path is implied. The investigation records the remaining messenger work: endpoint UX/storage, notifications, updates, abuse controls and group policy integration. If MLS fails a material gate, compare the documented libsignal alternative and return a concrete recommendation to the owner.

Signal integration and Bodferd trust#

This section is a proposed integration design, not an implemented Signal client. Sources were inspected on 2026-10-14. Keep the reporting CLI small. Stock Signal is excluded from the compliant candidate set; a libsignal investigation would assess an independent messenger, not a small stock-app integration. The owner selected MLS to lead the investigation, with libsignal retained as an alternative (A21); this section scopes that alternative. The strict Tor-only and automatic membership requirements are acceptance gates; a companion workflow that fails them is not the target solution.

What Signal code actually supplies#

libsignal contains the message protocol and related components, including private-group primitives. Its supported products for Signal's own use expose Java, Swift and TypeScript interfaces over Rust. Upstream explicitly says third-party use is unsupported and APIs can change. There is no established Go integration promised here. Pin a tested release/commit, isolate its bindings behind a narrow adapter, retain upstream tests and budget continued security-update work. No Signal dependency is installed by this design. libsignal source and support boundary.

Signal's server is also open source, but its sample configuration includes DynamoDB, Redis clusters, object storage, push and registration/recovery/contact-discovery dependencies in addition to FoundationDB. Group roster/control storage also lives in the separate storage-service application, which uses Bigtable and its own group controllers. A fork therefore needs an explicit inventory and operating plan for multiple services; deploying Signal-Server alone does not provide the complete product or operational setup. A source fork is not a turnkey private Signal deployment. Signal-Server build documentation.

The inspected libsignal and server projects use AGPLv3. Bodferd's current original documents and static reading code are MIT-licensed; that does not relicense incorporated Signal code. Choose a compatible distribution structure and satisfy the relevant upstream license before adding a dependency or fork. License selection for a combined messaging product remains a recorded decision. libsignal license.

A. Integrating with the existing Signal application#

A companion mode can verify a node-authorized Bodferd registration, then help an operator bind it to a Signal contact through a short-lived challenge answered within an encrypted conversation. Both participants independently compare the Signal safety number using the authenticated Bodferd relationship or another trusted channel. Safety numbers belong to a pair of contacts; they are not a universal node certificate. Reinstallations/key changes require renewed verification. A username, profile name or successful account challenge alone cannot establish the node-to-current-identity-key binding. Signal safety-number documentation.

Group administrators could inspect Bodferd credentials manually and remove members through Signal's normal controls. Signal supports private groups, administrator controls and optional approval of group-link join requests, which is not automatic credential enforcement. Signal group documentation.

This route preserves the existing app's UX and update path, but stock clients do not implement the proposed Bodferd credential rules. This design has not established a supported Signal bot, enrollment or group-management API. A companion label is advisory; it cannot compel an unmodified client to stop sharing group keys after a chain-role revocation. Do not put a decryption bot in every group to enforce membership: that gives the bot access to content and group relationships. Do not claim this route meets Tor-only transport without demonstrating every network path. Stock Signal fails the specified Tor-only transport and automatic membership gates and is excluded from implementation candidates. An account challenge is only an advisory association; no supported companion API binds a served identity key or enforces revocation. Its phone-number registration introduces identity disclosure outside the stated model. Users may separately choose stock Signal for ordinary communication, but that is outside Bodferd's confidentiality/transport contract; this design does not schedule a pilot claiming compliance.

B. A new messenger reusing libsignal cryptographic components#

The candidate architecture has three explicit boundaries:

LayerReuse / responsibilityAuthority boundary
Bodferd identity and policyVerify node relationships, developer attestations, device delegations and group permissionsAuthorizes identities/actions; possesses no conversation decryption key
Local messaging adapterPinned libsignal pairwise sessions/sender-key primitives, encrypted local state; a separately reviewed group applicationKeys remain on endpoints; application policy governs which devices receive them
Tor delivery and group storageBounded ciphertext queues, encrypted group state and protocol-native proof verification where adoptedRoutes data; cannot silently appoint developers, enroll devices or rewrite trusted policy

The first reporting CLI may remain Go. Option B requires a new client in TypeScript, Java or Swift using upstream bindings, or a separately justified Rust integration; it cannot reuse Go verification code in-process without a supported language boundary. Port the public verifier contract with cross-language fixtures rather than promise a nonexistent Go wrapper or invent security-sensitive IPC. libsignal supplies pairwise ratchets and sender-key distribution/cipher operations, not group lifecycle, authenticated rosters, device enrollment, notifications, attachment handling or encrypted local backups. Those require client/server application work and independent review; the reuse claim is limited to the imported cryptographic primitives. Do not build bespoke FFI, prekey or ratchet code as a shortcut. An independent network uses its own service identifiers and deployment; neither stock Signal-server compatibility nor access to Signal's production network is assumed.

Retain library-native authenticated session establishment and ratchet behavior instead of changing KDF inputs or mixing chain signatures into message encryption. Signal publishes PQXDH, ratchet and multi-device session specifications. Its 2 October 2025 SPQR announcement describes combining the Sparse Post Quantum Ratchet with Double Ratchet as the Triple Ratchet. Do not equate a 2026 dependency pin with the older Double Ratchet alone; the selected implementation/version and complete session lifecycle must establish the exact supported security properties. Forward secrecy and compromise recovery require correct state handling, key deletion and subsequent honest exchanges; changing a dependency name does not establish them. Group properties must be evaluated separately from pairwise ratchets. PQXDH specification, Double Ratchet specification, Sesame specification.

Bind trust to the actual device; do not alter the ratchet#

For the independent libsignal candidate, the proposed model uses a separate protocol identity key per Bodferd device, rather than Signal's account identity shared by linked devices. This is a departure from the deployed account/ACI/PNI model and needs demonstrated session/device interoperability before selection; it does not claim stock Signal compatibility. A device public-key hash covers SHA-256 of the exact library-native serialized identity public key (including its type byte), not an Ed25519 or age key. A proposed Bodferd messaging credential binds: application purpose/version, environment and chain, authorizer evidence, communication registration digest, parent scope, member ID, subject identifier, messaging device ID, hash of the protocol-native public identity key, credential sequence, issued/expiry times, issuer and explicit capabilities. The communication identity authorizes its device; independent policy grants developer/group-administrator roles. Demonstrate possession through the selected messaging protocol before activation. Do not assume libsignal identity keys are Ed25519, convert age identities, or reuse node secrets as ratchet material.

Peers verify the full binding and current authorization before establishing a trusted conversation. The UI shows provenance such as node-signature-verified or registrar-witnessed, role issuer, last chain-state check, expiry and device changes. A witnessed node binding never becomes a stronger label just because it travels through Signal encryption. A delivery server cannot swap an identity key while retaining the old certificate; clients reject mismatch rather than silently applying trust-on-first-use. The authenticated Bodferd credential is the authorization root; the messaging directory supplies routing/key material and cannot grant identity. Honest re-key blocks new sends until a newly authorized credential, device possession proof and authenticated peer/group update agree with the directory. Cache highest credential sequences and current revocation information; stale replay cannot overwrite them. Show a pending re-verification state instead of a warning bypass. Existing decrypted history remains local; offline credential expiry blocks privileged changes and new sessions. The enrollment/role issuer, not the directory, resolves replacement credentials.

Trust is a set of scoped facts and capabilities, not a global numeric score. Examples include current node operator, independently approved developer, member of a named response group and administrator of that group. A policy can require one or more of these facts. Active-to-Standby churn does not by itself remove an operator if both statuses satisfy policy; loss of the actual operator relationship affects the node-derived role, not unrelated independently issued roles. Refresh cadence, maximum staleness and offline behavior are explicit policy choices. Expired or uncertain authority blocks new privileged membership changes; no indefinite silent grace.

Enforce membership in clients and key distribution#

Group policy names eligible roles, permitted assurance levels, policy owner, invitation/removal rules, administrative threshold, visibility and history access. Approved invites bind the group, exact device identity keys, credential digests and expected group-state version. Clients validate them before distributing secrets. The messaging system's authenticated group state/control path carries the membership change; a plaintext badge or a SQL role update is insufficient.

Clients refuse unapproved device additions and policy changes, authenticate the resulting membership revision and stop new confidential sends when removal/key update is pending or views conflict. Role revocation removes all affected devices through the selected group protocol and stops distributing new sender/group secrets to them. Verify the concrete libsignal/client implementation's removal, key-rotation and queued-message behavior; private-group administration alone is not proof of group post-compromise security. Already authorized members can still retain or copy messages, forward secrets, or collude. A bot or server-side ACL cannot revoke previously learned plaintext.

Different read audiences use different encrypted groups. Giving every member the same decryption secret and hiding developer-only messages with a UI role check does not enforce confidentiality. The signed trust credential authenticates eligibility; it is not attached as a transferable node signature to every chat message. Incident reports remain durably signed. Bodferd identity/device credentials are transferable identity bindings, and sender-key group messages have verification signatures visible to members. This draft makes no cryptographic deniability promise for group conversation traffic or those credentials, even when pairwise encryption retains upstream Signal authentication properties. Do not add a node/report signature to each chat message; assess the chosen protocol's actual deniability separately and show the identity-binding limitation in product documentation.

Preserve group privacy rather than exposing roles to every server#

Signal's private-group design stores encrypted membership state and verifies credential presentations without learning the member identity from that presentation. Its libsignal zkgroup components are worth evaluating before building a central plaintext membership database. Keep custom role evidence inside encrypted group state, visible to entitled members, rather than publishing node/developer/group tuples for routing. Signal private-group system.

This is not an invitation to add arbitrary attributes to a zero-knowledge proof. The inspected upstream authentication API has specific identity/time inputs and verification against group parameters; it is not a generic constructor for node-bond or developer-role proofs. Reuse supported issuance/presentation formats. A chain-role credential can gate issuance or be checked by authorized clients, with its exact privacy and issuer knowledge documented. The holder of ServerSecretParams can issue credentials for supported UIDs and is an explicit authentication trust root. Issuer compromise, impersonation, issuance logs and collusion are review cases; group admission still requires authenticated device credentials and group-owner authorization, with no claim that proof privacy hides identities from the issuer. Custom zero-knowledge role proofs require independent cryptographic design and review. Upstream credential API.

Enrollment already knows the node; the report relay remains identity-aware. Future group delivery must separately assess whether issuance and presentation are linkable through accounts, capabilities, logs, timing or colluding services. Do not present separation of two services as unlinkability by itself. Signal's sealed-sender design targets sender metadata, but importing libsignal does not automatically enable it in a new transport. Tor hides network location; it does not erase identifying application headers or global timing correlation. Signal sealed-sender design.

What must still be built and verified#

Bodferd still owns endpoint storage, rollback-safe atomic session updates, bounded skipped-message keys, device recovery, invitations, abuse controls, attachments, notifications, updates and supply-chain verification. Queue retry/replay handling cannot restore old ratchet state or reuse consumed prekeys. Avoid key-bearing backups that undermine forward secrecy. Do not add message-content telemetry, directory dumps or clearnet fallback. A known-good library protects the primitives; the integration and endpoints can still compromise them.

Before selecting this path, the investigation must demonstrate two operators and a developer group; offline and out-of-order delivery; authenticated device replacement; rejection of substituted devices and stale credentials; concurrent membership changes; multi-device removal with fresh key distribution; crash/restart recovery without state rollback; Tor-only background traffic; and a server compromise that reveals no message plaintext. Record which metadata each server/issuer can see. Assess the pinned component's group security independently, update burden and license compatibility. Keep libsignal-client and MLS alternatives open until this evidence distinguishes them; stock Signal is excluded from the compliant candidate set; no implementation stack is approved by this document.

Remaining implementation prerequisites#

The corrected draft still needs an independent re-check. Before implementation readiness, prove the on-chain policy carrier and complete freshness-verification route. These external facts also remain unverified: actual maintainer/registrar identities and fingerprints; permission/access for any future Discord integration; original signed-envelope export from supported node releases; wallet sign-only format compatibility; independent chain verifier availability and historical-state retention; dedicated onion provisioning; provider attachment/TLS limits; pilot resource/retention suitability. Container framing is specified above; interoperable implementation fixtures remain required validation work.

None requires substituting a weaker claim. Prefer direct cryptographic enrollment; witnessed make relay is available only with explicitly authorized registrar trust. Bootstrap maintainer roles independently. Ship initially to the synthetic test environment, verify all controls, and then provision production through the repository release process when requested. This document does not activate services, publish keys, register users, send mail or authorize use of unprovisioned production secrets.

The owner decisions and accepted availability/metadata risks are recorded in review-decisions.md. Draft dispositions are not independent findings closure; the original external reviewer must re-check them against this revision.

Adversarial review

The original findings remain open until implementation and verification establish that the controls work.

Download the findings register

Reviewed 2026-10-14. This reviews the user's proposed CLI/service design, not an implemented relay. Findings describe design risks, not demonstrated vulnerabilities in an implemented Bodferd service. Independent identity and cryptography/privacy reviews informed this register; recommendations below are application design judgments.

Scope and verdict#

Proposal: a node operator signs a communication using a node/operator key, encrypts a file locally with age after checking the recipient against the service, uploads over Tor, and the service validates it before emailing itzamna@thorchain.org. Testing uses pfc@pfc.zone.

The architecture is viable for confidential, authenticated submissions. The stated requirement that an opaque relay verify correct encryption needs revision. Recipient trust, exact signature semantics, replay protection, node authorization, delivery semantics, and recipient handling must be specified before implementation.

Intended boundaries:

  • The relay sees the submitting node identity and admission metadata, but has no report decryption key.
  • The maintainer sees the report and its verified sender identity.
  • Email systems see delivery metadata and retain ciphertext; they should not see report contents or node identity.
  • Tor reduces network-location exposure. It does not make a signed node submission anonymous to the relay.
  • Compromise of the submitting machine or the maintainer's decryption environment can disclose plaintext. Compromise of the relay can disclose admission metadata, disrupt delivery, or issue dishonest receipts.

No actual recipient public key, maintainer key confirmation, current node-launcher version, or email-provider arrangement was supplied. Those are prerequisites, not facts established by this review.

Findings register#

R01 — Critical: correct encryption is not publicly verifiable with ordinary age#

Component attacked: server validates that the file is properly encrypted to the maintainer.

Argument: a public-key-only relay can check bounded format and a signed declaration, but ordinary age does not provide a proof of recipient decryptability or full ciphertext integrity. A signature over garbage remains a valid signature. Giving the relay the maintainer's private key destroys the intended confidentiality boundary.

Evidence: the age format authenticates the header and payload using secret material. Native X25519 stanzas do not disclose the recipient public key. Tagged recipient types support recipient matching, but matching alone does not authenticate the payload.

Remediation: promise “authorized sender, declared recipient policy, bounded age-format ciphertext,” with full decryption verification at the maintainer. Do not label syntax inspection “encryption verified.” A stronger publicly verifiable encryption requirement would need a separately reviewed cryptographic scheme, not a header check. A malicious sender already controls their plaintext; no client protocol prevents them sharing it elsewhere.

R02 — Critical: checking a key against the service is circular trust#

Component attacked: local encryption recipient confirmed using the relay's stored key.

Argument: if that service supplies and approves an attacker's key, the CLI can confidentially send the report to the attacker while appearing successful.

Evidence: no independent trust anchor is present in the proposal. Onion authentication authenticates the chosen service, not its assertions about a maintainer key.

Remediation: independently confirm the maintainer's key. Pin an offline policy-signing root in authenticated CLI releases. Serve a signed policy binding recipient public key/fingerprint, maintainer identity, environment, onion identity, policy version, validity, and revocations. Verify it locally before encryption; reject rollback, expiry, disagreement, and unapproved changes. Remember the highest accepted policy version. Specify root recovery and revocation publication; a compromised relay can withhold a newer policy, so use short validity and an independent refresh path. Never provide a routine “ignore mismatch” option.

R00 — High: existing make relay broadcasts rather than only signing#

Component attacked: reuse make relay as the signing step for confidential submissions.

Argument: the existing command prepares and broadcasts a message through the Discord relay workflow. Calling it with report text can publish confidential text through the wrong service; even publishing ciphertext exposes identity and timing. It is not a local sign-only primitive.

Evidence: the launcher wrapper passes channel/message to the node wrapper. The current THORNode query command calls Prepare() and Broadcast(). Its relay implementation fetches a UUID prefix, signs UUID|Channel|Text, and posts to the configured relay using ordinary Go HTTP calls with no explicit Tor transport. The current default configuration names the existing Discord relay service. Source was inspected through public GitLab raw/API reads; this does not establish the version/configuration installed on a particular operator's node or the existing relay server's replay guarantees.

Remediation: implement a separate local sign-only adapter with a restricted purpose and inspectable payload. Never pass confidential report text to the existing broadcast command. The signing helper uses the Cosmos account keyring signer; distinguish that account key from validator consensus and TSS/vault keys. Specify and test signature compatibility with the actual supported node release rather than assuming a generic wallet signature is interchangeable.

R03 — High: a valid signature does not establish node/operator authorization#

Component attacked: signer is a valid node operator.

Argument: anyone can create a key and produce a cryptographically valid signature. The supplied public key must be mapped to authoritative THORChain state. A provider funding a pooled node must not automatically be treated as its operator.

Evidence: official THORNode Stack documentation distinguishes node signing material from the operator key and says make relay uses node material. The Node Operations API example separately lists node keys, operator address, bond providers, and status.

Remediation: define node-key and operator-key verification paths separately. Pin the supported network/chain ID and signature format. Derive the signer's account address from its verified public key; authorize the exact node Cosmos account or on-chain node_operator_address, not a claimed address or any bond provider. Check that relationship against fresh, trusted chain state. Prefer an independently operated full node; multiple REST providers are a trust heuristic, not cryptographic state verification. Do not trust the submitting node's own membership claim. Record the validation height and define staleness/unavailability behavior. Allow one operator to correspond to multiple nodes without multiplying quotas accidentally.

R04 — High: routine CLI use can endanger powerful keys#

Component attacked: CLI calls the node or operator signer on every report.

Argument: a vulnerable or malicious binary installed near validator secrets can do more than sign a report. A publicly reachable arbitrary signing API creates another attack surface. Node and operator keys have different consequences on compromise.

Evidence: the Stack documentation associates these keys with chain operations; the proposal has no signer isolation or restricted authorization scope.

Remediation: prefer a dedicated communication key authorized by a short-lived, domain-separated delegation certificate signed locally by the node/operator key. Bind node identity, delegate key, audience, network, environment, allowed action, expiry, certificate ID, and quotas. Recheck the parent authorization at submission. Define delegate revocation and independent emergency denial, including what happens after parent compromise. Keep the node helper small and local: no remote scripts, mnemonic export, generic remote signing endpoint, or arbitrary shell command accepted from the relay. Use authenticated releases and offline signing support.

R05 — High: insufficient signature binding permits attachment substitution and misuse#

Component attacked: sign the communication, then attach a file.

Argument: signing a greeting or challenge does not authorize the uploaded bytes. An ambiguous encoding or missing destination/environment can allow reuse in another context.

Evidence: no signed payload schema is specified. The age author's authentication discussion distinguishes encryption integrity from sender authentication and identifies problems in naive signing/encryption composition.

Remediation: sign an unambiguous versioned manifest containing protocol purpose, service identity, network, environment, sender/delegation, recipient policy digest, ciphertext SHA-256 and byte length, submission ID, one-use challenge, and expiry. Specify exact canonical bytes and algorithms; reject duplicate keys, unsupported fields/versions, and noncanonical encodings. Use a distinct domain for delegation, content authorship, submission admission, and receipts. Do not publish a transaction-shaped signature or rely on a delimiter-concatenated string.

R06 — High: signing ciphertext alone does not prove authorship of its plaintext#

Component attacked: uploaded file originated from the signing operator.

Argument: another authorized sender can sign copied ciphertext without knowing its contents. Submission authorization and content authorship are different assertions.

Evidence: the age author's discussion explicitly identifies this issue in encrypt-then-sign composition.

Remediation: inside the encrypted package, include a signed content manifest covering the message, file hashes/lengths, submission ID, intended maintainer/policy, network, and environment. The maintainer must check agreement between inner author and outer submitter, or an explicitly authorized forwarding relationship. Neither signature alone should be described as proving human intent. Obtain review of this application protocol before release.

R07 — High: replay protection must survive retries, concurrency, and restarts#

Component attacked: a validated submission triggers an email.

Argument: captured valid submissions can otherwise produce repeated delivery. Process-local nonce storage disappears on rollout. Concurrent requests can both pass a naive check.

Evidence: the proposal has no replay state, atomic acceptance, or retry behavior.

Remediation: use unpredictable, short-lived challenges bound to the manifest's identity, recipient policy, and submission. Maintain durable submission IDs and atomic nonce consumption plus queue insertion after complete verification. An identical retry returns the previous receipt; different bytes with the same ID fail. Limit pending reservations and clean up unfinished uploads. Retain replay records for the full acceptance window. SMTP delivery is separate and may duplicate after an uncertain network result; recipient tooling deduplicates using the signed submission ID.

R08 — High: node status policy can exclude operators during the incident being reported#

Component attacked: valid-node requirement.

Argument: “active validators only” can exclude a churned-out or jailed node reporting an attack. “Any historical node” can admit indefinitely compromised or abandoned identities.

Evidence: THORChain node status changes through churn; the proposal leaves eligibility undefined.

Remediation: specify accepted statuses and a bounded recently-authorized recovery category. Distinguish trust levels in the encrypted evidence. If emergency unauthenticated reporting is needed, give it a separate limited lane with an explicit unverified label. Never silently fall back to accepting unverifiable node identity when chain verification fails.

R09 — High: Tor transport does not conceal signed node identity#

Component attacked: privacy of the operator.

Argument: the relay needs a node-linked identity to enforce the proposed admission rule. It can correlate submissions, and public node records may associate that identity with a node IP. Signed reports also create transferable evidence if disclosed.

Evidence: node identity is part of the proposed verification. Tor's onion-service explanation describes location hiding and service authentication, not anonymization of identifying application data.

Remediation: state “node-authenticated and confidential; relay knows node identity.” Reduce retained identity data. If identity must be hidden from the relay, move verification to the maintainer or design unlinkable admission credentials as a separate project. A delegated communication key still identifies its parent through its certificate.

R10 — High: email leaks metadata and creates durable copies#

Component attacked: encrypted attachment emailed to maintainer.

Argument: encrypting only the attachment leaves subject, message, filename, node identity, reply address, timing, and size exposed where used in ordinary email fields. Mail archives and forwarding multiply ciphertext copies.

Evidence: the proposal does not define encrypted message boundaries. These leaks follow from plaintext mail headers and attachment metadata.

Remediation: encrypt the whole report, including message and original filenames. Use a generic fixed subject, relay From address, randomized generic attachment name, fixed configured destination, and no operator Reply-To. Wrap the complete submission manifest, signatures, delegation and ciphertext in an additional age envelope for email, so providers do not see node identity. The relay needs only the pinned public recipient key for this outer envelope. Providers still see size, timing, relay and recipient. Padding inside encryption and optional batching reduce easy correlation at a cost in bandwidth and urgency. Prefer an onion mailbox plus generic email notification when metadata minimization matters more than attached-email convenience.

R11 — High: static recipient keys do not provide forward secrecy#

Component attacked: long-term confidentiality of stored reports.

Argument: theft of a maintainer's decryption key exposes retained historical ciphertext encrypted to that key. Rotation does not undo exposure while old keys/copies remain.

Evidence: this follows from static-key encryption and retained SMTP copies; the age author's article distinguishes forward secrecy from its ordinary encryption use.

Remediation: isolate decryption from the upload/mail service, protect identities and backups, minimize retention, and practice key-loss/compromise recovery. Consider supported hybrid post-quantum age recipients for long-lived incident material after interoperability testing; upstream age documentation documents support in v1.3.0+. Post-quantum encryption does not solve key theft or provide forward secrecy. A true forward-secrecy requirement needs a different reviewed protocol/key lifecycle.

R12 — High: testing can misroute confidential production reports#

Component attacked: test recipient pfc@pfc.zone, production recipient itzamna@thorchain.org.

Argument: an email-only switch can send ciphertext to the wrong person, or reuse a test decryption key in production. Client-controlled recipients create an open mail relay or exfiltration route.

Evidence: test and production routing are named but their key/environment separation is unspecified.

Remediation: use distinct signed policies, age keys, service identities, configuration, credentials and queues. Bind environment and recipient policy in signatures. Fix the destination server-side; reject client overrides, CC/BCC, arbitrary subject/headers, callbacks, or URLs to fetch. Test only with synthetic data. Production should refuse to start with test configuration and vice versa. Independently confirm each intended recipient possesses the corresponding identity.

R13 — High: authorized senders and unauthenticated uploads can exhaust the service#

Component attacked: public onion upload and mail dispatch.

Argument: signatures do not prevent anonymous bandwidth floods or a legitimate/compromised node flooding maintainers. Tor peers are unsuitable as meaningful per-operator IP quota keys.

Evidence: no resource limits are proposed. Tor's onion DoS guidance recommends service-level defenses; these do not replace application limits.

Remediation: admit a small signed manifest first, verify eligibility/quota, and issue a short-lived capability for a bounded upload. Still enforce global connection, byte, time, CPU, challenge and spool limits. Stream ciphertext to bounded storage; do not buffer unbounded bodies. Enforce quotas by parent operator/node and globally, bound worker retries, and reserve incident capacity. Tor client authorization is optional if onboarding permits it. Treat Tor PoW as congestion mitigation, not proof of node identity.

R14 — High: encrypted hostile files endanger the maintainer#

Component attacked: recipient opens a validated attachment.

Argument: encryption prevents relay content scanning. A valid-node signature does not make a file safe, and reported logs can contain secrets or attacker-controlled strings.

Evidence: authentication authenticates a key, not the safety or truthfulness of content.

Remediation: provide recipient verification/decryption tooling. Stage output until full integrity and required signature checks finish; discard partial output after any failure. Do not auto-open, execute, preview HTML, fetch links, or extract archives. If extraction is offered, reject traversal, symlinks and resource bombs. Review reports in a restricted environment. Offer local inspection/redaction for mnemonics, keys, credentials and identifying log data; do not automatically gather node backup/key directories.

R15 — High: relay receipts cannot prove maintainer delivery#

Component attacked: successful upload means delivered report.

Argument: a compromised relay can drop the report and claim success. An SMTP server accepting responsibility does not prove the maintainer read or decrypted it.

Evidence: SMTP RFC 5321 specifies transfer of delivery responsibility and subsequent failures, not human acknowledgement.

Remediation: distinguish accepted, queued, SMTP accepted, failed, and maintainer acknowledged. Return a signed receipt binding submission ID and ciphertext hash. Permit private status polling using a high-entropy capability in a header, with limited retention; do not place it in logged URLs. An end-to-end acknowledgement should be signed with a separately trusted maintainer acknowledgement key and bind the submission hash. It can be polled over Tor or encrypted to a one-time reply recipient. Never imply a relay receipt removes censorship risk.

R16 — High: sharing an unrelated backend enlarges the confidentiality boundary#

Component attacked: deployment alongside the current swap application.

Argument: unrelated app compromise could expose node identities, queues or mail credentials. Onion reachability alone does not make a shared backend inaccessible over other paths.

Evidence: no Bodferd backend has been deployed. This is a proposed deployment threat: sharing public ingress, execution, storage or unrelated signing credentials enlarges the attack surface. HTTP method restrictions do not provide durable isolation for a confidential upload service.

Remediation: prefer a dedicated relay deployment, onion identity, storage, Tor client/service and minimal mail worker. No public ingress, public load balancer, or dependency on untrusted Host/forwarded headers for Tor-only admission. Restrict backend reachability with enforceable network policy or a same-host private socket. Use independent credentials, least privilege, non-root execution, resource caps, ciphertext-only bounded queues, and minimal logs. Follow this repo's SOPS-only rule for service secrets. Keep the maintainer age identity off the cluster.

R17 — Medium: a proxy setting alone is not a reliable Tor-only client guarantee#

Component attacked: local Tor relay required for communication.

Argument: clients need a Tor client/daemon, not to operate a public Tor relay. Proxy bypass, redirects, direct diagnostics, DNS, update checks and telemetry can reveal activity.

Evidence: Tor's SOCKS extensions describe hostname addressing and stream isolation. Tor's limitations include timing correlation.

Remediation: explicitly connect to a configured local SOCKS endpoint, pass the pinned onion hostname through SOCKS, reject redirects and direct fallback, disable telemetry and automatic network update checks, and apply supported stream isolation. A high-assurance mode should enforce network access to only the local Tor endpoint, while preserving explicit local/offline signing. Do not promise resistance to an observer monitoring both ends. Padding/batching do not eliminate this threat.

R18 — High: open source does not establish trust in downloaded binaries#

Component attacked: public CLI running near sensitive operator material.

Argument: a compromised release, dependency or installer can steal plaintext before encryption or misuse signer access. This bypasses the protocol entirely.

Evidence: the proposal specifies open source but no distribution verification.

Remediation: use a small CLI, preferably Go given available age/THORChain libraries; select audited compatible versions rather than implementing primitives. Pin dependencies, publish authenticated checksums/build provenance and reproducible build instructions, isolate release signing, and prohibit shell-piped installers. Upstream age provides Sigsum release proofs. Keep network submission separable from local signing so an operator can inspect exactly what is authorized. Review the protocol and parsers independently before production.

Recommended flow for the first implementation#

  1. Independently bootstrap policy-root trust, onion identity, supported chain and maintainer recipient key. Configure production and test separately.
  2. Generate a communication key locally. Authorize it using a narrow, expiring node/operator delegation. Direct signing can be an explicit fallback with the same admission semantics.
  3. Fetch and locally verify the signed current recipient policy over Tor; check it against the client's trust and rollback state.
  4. Create a submission ID. Package the message, file, original metadata and inner signed content manifest locally. Encrypt that package using the approved age recipient. Finalize immutable ciphertext, hash it and measure its length.
  5. Obtain a bounded one-use admission challenge over Tor. Sign the canonical outer manifest binding that challenge, ciphertext and destination policy.
  6. Relay verifies the manifest, fresh node/operator authorization, delegation, expiry and quotas before granting upload capacity. On complete upload it verifies exact size/hash and bounded age structure. Atomically accept and queue; return a receipt. It cannot attest successful maintainer decryption.
  7. Mail worker uses a fixed destination and pinned public key to encrypt the complete original submission bundle into a generic mail attachment. Forward the original signatures and delegation, not just a relay's validation assertion.
  8. Maintainer tooling unwraps the mail envelope, checks the original admission signature and authorization evidence against its own trust, decrypts the report, then verifies the inner manifest and file hashes before presenting content. Validation expiry refers to acceptance time, not arbitrary delayed reading time. An optional signed acknowledgement returns through private Tor polling.

Verification cases required before shipping#

  • Arbitrary self-generated signers, unrelated bond providers, stale/wrong chain state, wrong network, churn/status boundaries, parent revocation and expired delegates.
  • Policy substitution, downgrade, expiry, rotation and offline-root recovery; cross-environment key and email routing.
  • Modified ciphertext, truncation, wrong declared size, malformed headers, unsupported recipient types, ambiguous manifests, duplicate JSON keys and mismatched inner/outer authors.
  • Concurrent replay, retries after lost responses, restart/rollout persistence, incomplete uploads, uncertain SMTP acceptance and recipient deduplication.
  • Large/slow uploads, challenge floods, compromised authorized-node floods, full queues and storage exhaustion.
  • Tor failure produces no direct connection; clearnet/backend paths cannot submit; redirects are rejected; logs contain no report body, identity-bearing signature or private status capability by default.
  • Recipient rejects partial decryption and unsafe extraction. Missing maintainer keys fail visibly. SMTP acceptance and end-to-end acknowledgement remain distinct.
  • Relay compromise simulation cannot decrypt an existing valid client-encrypted report or substitute an independently trusted recipient key. It can still suppress delivery and observe admission metadata; document that residual risk.

Remediation path#

First settle encryption-validation semantics, recipient trust, signer eligibility and the privacy promise. Then specify exact manifest/delegation/receipt formats and recipient handling; only then implement CLI, isolated service and synthetic test deployment. This review creates documentation only. No application/cluster changes, commits, pushes, tags, PRs or test emails were performed. Repository instructions reserve PR creation/merging to the user and prohibit GitHub CLI/MCP, so the durable local report is the review handoff.

Follow-up, 2026-10-14: the user requested integration of the findings with public make relay key registration and selected protocol design before implementation. The controlling node relay protocol maps all ten summarized controls to mechanisms and acceptance evidence, separates age encryption from communication signing, and distinguishes original node signatures from registrar-witnessed Discord enrollment. These are designed controls, not implemented remediations; this review's findings remain open until implementation and verification evidence exist.

External review and dispositions

The supplied review is preserved. Dispositions describe draft revisions; independent re-check and implementation evidence remain outstanding.

Download external review · Read the owner's decisions

Reviewed 2026-10-14 against commit b5e701e (main). Corpus: docs/design.md (controlling design), docs/security-review.md (original register R00–R18), src/overview.html, src/shell.html, src/read.js, scripts/build.mjs, dist/, README.md, PRODUCT.md, docs/streams/, .impeccable/finish-review.md. Nothing is implemented; every finding below is a design or documentation defect, not a demonstrated vulnerability in a running service.

Method: five independent review passes (protocol composition, trust model, Signal/MLS feasibility, website and build, operational feasibility), then a skeptical re-read of every finding against the source by the coordinating reviewer. Findings that the design already handles were dropped; a list of those is at the end. Where two passes reached a finding independently it is marked (corroborated). Inline annotations in the reviewed files are wrapped in Z>>> … <<<Z and reference the IDs below; strip them with perl -0pi -e 's/\n?Z>>>.*?<<<Z\n?//sg' <file> or perl -0pi -e 's/<!-- Z>>>.*?<<<Z -->\n?//sg' <file> for HTML.

Verdict#

The v1 reporting protocol is unusually careful about what it refuses to promise, and its mechanics (signature domain separation, outer/inner manifests, status capability, honest receipt vocabulary) are sound. It fails as an incident-reporting system on three structural points the text never confronts: (1) an operator who has not pre-enrolled cannot report at all, and the only enrollment path that exists today needs two human registrars and up to 48 hours; (2) every "independent" trust root is unnamed and, in the only configuration anyone can provision today, resolves to the proposer; (3) a 24-hour policy expiry signed by an offline two-party authority turns a daily ceremony into a single point of failure that is most likely to fail during a crisis. The Signal section is well-hedged sentence by sentence but keeps two options alive (stock-Signal companion, libsignal client) that its own gates already rule out, while under-weighting the option (MLS) that fits its constraints. The website is honest in its status notes and then undoes that in a facts box and a controls paragraph that read as achieved state.

Severity key: Critical = the system would not serve its stated purpose or the stated security claim is false; High = a security or availability property is unmet or two implementers would build incompatible/insecure results; Medium = unspecified behaviour with a plausible bad outcome; Low = hygiene, wording, latent.

Findings register#

A01 — Critical: there is no way for a non-enrolled operator to report an active incident (corroborated: ops, trust, website)#

Component attacked: the incident-time user journey; the dropped R08 emergency lane.

Argument: Before a first report send, an operator must have: a verified CLI and out-of-band policy fingerprint; a local Tor daemon; identity create; a fetched, threshold-verified policy; a registration challenge; authorizer evidence; possession proofs for both keys inside a 10-minute window; and a passing chain-eligibility check. The preferred evidence path (sign-only adapter or envelope exporter) does not exist today by the design's own admission, so every real enrollment goes through an unmodified public make relay post plus two policy-authorized registrars attesting within 48 hours. Those registrars are not provisioned either. R08 explicitly asked for "a separate limited lane with an explicit unverified label" for emergency reporting; the design provides only a status-recovery attestation for Disabled nodes and a hard "never fall back" rule. An operator watching funds drain will DM a maintainer on Discord, which is what the system exists to replace. The design also never states its operating assumption: operators must enroll in advance, and someone must run an enrollment campaign, and until an upstream sign-only or export primitive ships, production enrollment is registrar-witnessed only.

Evidence: docs/design.md:117 "No signature-export functionality is assumed to exist today."; :103 "witnessed enrollment allows 48 hours for human approvals"; :118 "Production proposal: two distinct policy-authorized registrars"; :126 "Never fall back to anonymous acceptance after failed chain verification."; :399 registrar identities, exporter, adapter and chain verifier all "remain unverified"; docs/security-review.md:111 (R08 remediation).

Remediation: Add a labelled, rate-limited, unauthenticated-or-weakly-authenticated emergency lane (e.g. any current on-chain node key signing a short message, no registration) that the maintainer tool displays as unverified. State in the design that launch runs on the witnessed path only and budget the registrar roster. Make "pre-enrollment campaign" an explicit prerequisite.

A02 — Critical: every "independent" trust root is unnamed and, as provisionable today, resolves to the proposer (corroborated: trust, ops)#

Component attacked: :38 "Independent offline administrators"; :47 "trust bundle independently of the relay"; :64 "Only the independent authority establishes that role"; :9 "independently trusted maintainer policy".

Argument: The design names nobody. The relay is to run in the proposer's estate, the test mailbox is the proposer's domain, the repository owner chooses the roster, and no maintainer-side party participates in the design. If one organisation holds both threshold keys, runs the relay and staffs the registrar seats, the 2-of-N threshold protects against losing one key file, not against that organisation: it can issue a policy naming an attacker-controlled report_age_recipient and every pinned CLI will encrypt to it while reporting success, which is exactly the R02 circularity the policy layer was built to break. The trust bundle ships inside the signed CLI release, so the release-signing key (unnamed, future work) is the de facto root above the policy authority. The "out-of-band" fingerprint channel is never named, and the only public channel mentioned (Discord) is one the design says cannot confer authority. Revocations reach clients only via GET /v1/policy on the relay. The maintainer's identity (itzamna@thorchain.org) is a user-supplied string; nothing requires the maintainer to publish a fingerprint through a channel operators already trust (e.g. a key known from thornode releases) or to countersign the policy. The policy authority also authorises the acknowledgement key, so it, not the relay, can forge "reviewed" acknowledgements.

Evidence: docs/design.md:13, :38, :47, :49, :56, :64, :66, :233, :251, :255; CLAUDE.md "the requesting repository owner chooses account/role roster identities".

Remediation: Write a separation rule into the policy schema and the design: no threshold signer may administer the relay; at least one production signer must be from the THORChain maintainer side; the maintainer countersigns the policy entry that names their key. Name the release-signing identity, the transparency/provenance mechanism (R18 pointed at Sigsum) and the out-of-band fingerprint channel. Name an independent publication location for policy and revocations that the relay cannot withhold.

A03 — High: a 24-hour policy expiry signed by an offline 2-of-N authority is a daily ceremony and a crisis-time outage (corroborated: ops, protocol, trust)#

Component attacked: :66 "Production policies expire within 24 hours by proposed default."

Argument: The whole policy object, including expires_at and the relay receipt keys, is threshold-signed by "independent offline administrators". Clients refuse to encrypt and the relay refuses to admit after expiry, with no bypass. That is two humans with offline keys signing every day forever; if they are unavailable for 48 hours (most likely during the incident that makes them busy) all incident reporting stops, and recovery requires "an independently verified replacement bundle". Rotating the relay receipt key is another offline ceremony. The design also leaves undefined what happens to immutable ciphertext encrypted under policy N and retried after policy N+1 (same recipient key, different policy_sha256); :68 covers accepted submissions only. The registration record's policy_sha256 (:93) is stale for most of its 30-day life and nothing says what it is compared to. "Independent publication" of updates (:66) names no channel, so every refresh is the relay.

Evidence: docs/design.md:38, :49, :51-60, :62, :66, :68, :93, :162, :171, :179, :233.

Remediation: Separate long-lived threshold-signed authority (roster, recipient keys, revocations; weeks to months) from short-lived freshness (an online, relay-independent, single-key-signed "current policy sequence" heartbeat or a published revocation feed). Define retry behaviour across policy sequences explicitly: accept if the recipient key is unchanged and the old policy is within a historical-verification window.

A04 — High: one maintainer, one mailbox, one age key, no continuity#

Component attacked: :56 singular maintainer: {…}; :43 "One report recipient is the default."

Argument: The policy schema has exactly one maintainer object and no roster. (:43 forbids silently adding a sender recovery recipient; it says nothing about a maintainer continuity recipient, but none is designed.) If the maintainer is unavailable or loses the age identity, every report is sealed to a key nobody can use; the relay has already deleted its ciphertext after SMTP acceptance; re-encryption needs the sender's cooperation. Acknowledgement is optional, so an operator cannot distinguish "being triaged" from "nobody has looked". The threshold exists only for policy signers, not for the people who read reports.

Evidence: docs/design.md:43, :56, :68, :268, :13.

Remediation: Make maintainer a list with explicit "any-of" decryption (multiple age recipients in the header is supported by age and is not the group-chat anti-pattern :304 warns about when the set is a policy-signed roster), an on-call/handoff statement, and a required received acknowledgement SLA in the test environment.

A05 — High: the registration digest and the parent signing input are ambiguous; two implementers will not interoperate (corroborated: protocol; website noted the consequence)#

Component attacked: :103 "hashes the non-challenge registration fields"; :105 "SHA-256 over canonical UTF-8 JSON"; :117 "signs the registration digest with a fixed application purpose".

Argument: The record schema includes challenge_id, challenge_nonce, issued_at, expires_at. Line 105 hashes the record; line 103 says the relay challenge hashes the non-challenge fields; so two digests exist and the text never says which one the node key signs, which goes into the THOR-RELAY-REGISTER-V1 marker, and which the possession statement carries. If the parent signs the full-record digest, every challenge retry (15-minute window) invalidates an already-posted Discord announcement. "Canonical UTF-8 JSON" at :105 is not stated to be the RFC 8785 JCS required at :140; previous_registration_sha256: "" vs absent is not pinned. For the parent (Cosmos secp256k1) signature, no byte format, hash mode or envelope is given (ADR-036 sign-arbitrary? raw purpose||digest? digest as pre-hash?); signing a 32-byte digest as a pre-hash is a cross-protocol hazard with Cosmos transaction signing.

Evidence: docs/design.md:94-97, :103, :105, :108, :117, :124, :140, :229, :399.

Remediation: Define registration_core (no challenge fields) and registration_full; state that the parent signs registration_core_sha256, the marker carries it, the comms-key possession statement signs registration_full_sha256 || challenge. Pin the parent signing envelope (recommend ADR-036 MsgSignData with a fixed signer and a domain-prefixed data payload), the accepted key algorithms and the address derivation.

A06 — High: in the witnessed path the real verifier is the THORChain Discord relay server operator, who is never listed as a trusted party (corroborated: trust, ops)#

Component attacked: :118 registrar-witnessed enrollment.

Argument: The chain of custody is node signature → existing THORChain relay server verifies and posts → Discord stores → bot message → registrars attest. The relay-server operator (THORChain devops, a third party) performs the only signature verification in that chain and appears in neither the key table nor the privacy promise. The attestation binds guild/channel/bot/message IDs, which does defeat webhook impersonation if registrars check the author's application ID; the design should say so. Two registrars protect against one registrar lying, not against a common forged or compromised feed, and if both are from the same organisation (A02) they protect against nothing. Registrar availability, paging and key custody are not described, and this is the path every production registration will use (A01).

Evidence: docs/design.md:31-39, :11, :118, :120, :257.

Remediation: Add the relay-server/bot operator to the trusted-party table with what it can do (admit a forged announcement). Require registrars to verify author application ID, not display name. Require registrars from at least two organisations in the production policy.

A07 — High: "retained trustworthy history" has no retainer, and the chain-state source is probably the relay operator's own node (corroborated: trust, protocol)#

Component attacked: :194 "Validate admission-time authorization using retained trustworthy history"; :33/:101/:128 "independent chain state"; :286 Row 6 "fresh state".

Argument: Verifying months later that node X had node_operator_address Y at height H requires archive state; THORNode defaults prune, and :399 admits historical retention is unverified. No party is assigned to retain it. If the relay retains it, the maintainer's step 2 is checking relay-produced evidence against relay-produced history, which contradicts "A relay's 'verified' label is insufficient". The realistic chain source is the proposer's own THORNode: independent of the submitter, not of the relay. The outer manifest records no validation height, so a lagging or forked relay node can admit a recently removed node with nothing in the evidence bundle showing the height used. R03 asked for recorded height and staleness bounds; Row 6 claims "fresh state" as the owning mechanism without either.

Evidence: docs/design.md:33, :101, :118, :128, :166-175, :194, :286, :399; docs/security-review.md:61.

Remediation: Add validation_height, validation_time and chain_source_id to the admission receipt and bundle; define maximum staleness; assign history retention (maintainer-side archive node or a signed snapshot feed) and state that the maintainer verifies against its own source.

A08 — High: email is an unchosen, unowned, spam-shaped transport that the original review recommended against#

Component attacked: mail worker; the decision to keep SMTP.

Argument: 10 MiB ciphertext plus 256 KiB metadata plus the outer age wrapper plus base64 is roughly 14 MB on the wire; that passes Gmail but fails common 10 MB corporate inbound limits, and no provider has been chosen for either domain. A relay From address needs a domain with SMTP credentials and SPF/DKIM/DMARC alignment; the design does not say whose domain or whose credentials, and k8s/creds/ is a human-gated risk path. The resulting mail (unknown sender, generic subject, random-named opaque binary, no text) is the textbook spam-quarantine profile, and there is no bounce/NDR handling beyond "quarantine visibly". The maintainer already runs the CLI over Tor to acknowledge or reply, so an onion pull of the bundle costs nothing extra and removes the provider, the credentials, the size limit and the permanent third-party copy. R10 said "Prefer an onion mailbox plus generic email notification"; the design keeps attached email without recording why.

Evidence: docs/design.md:13, :185, :189, :209, :264; docs/security-review.md:131; CLAUDE.md risk paths.

Remediation: Record the transport decision explicitly. Recommended: onion pull by the maintainer tool as primary, email as a content-free notification only.

A09 — High: onion key, registration DB, replay DB and revocation marks have no custody, backup or disaster-recovery design#

Component attacked: deployment and retention sections; :273 "Do not include report spools in routine backups".

Argument: The onion hostname is the service_id pinned in every registration, manifest and policy; "No certificate authorizes … outside its fixed service". Losing or rotating the onion key therefore re-enrolls the whole operator base through the 48-hour path, yet onion key custody, HA/OnionBalance and Tor daemon upgrades are never mentioned. The design requires durable replay and admission state and then says spools are excluded from backups, without saying what is backed up: the registration table, consumed-challenge store, 90-day tombstones and the revocation high-water marks that must "outlive removed certificates". A host loss with no restore makes revoked keys valid again. There is no runbook for relay operational-key rotation (it is "short-lived policy-authorized", so every rotation is an A03 ceremony).

Evidence: docs/design.md:39, :83, :134, :181, :253, :255, :273.

Remediation: Add a custody/backup/DR subsection: what state is durable, what is backed up and how (encrypted, off-cluster), onion key escrow under the same SOPS rule, and a migration procedure for service_id change that re-uses existing parent authorization.

A10 — High: the libsignal client option is building a messenger, and its device credential does not match Signal's per-account identity key (Signal pass; Go/FFI contradiction corroborated by protocol pass)#

Component attacked: :339 "including private-group primitives"; :360 "Pinned libsignal session/group primitives"; :363 Go CLI, no bespoke FFI; :369 device credential binds "messaging device ID, hash of the protocol-native public identity key"; :379 "Role revocation removes all affected devices".

Argument: In libsignal, group messaging is a sender-key cipher plus distribution messages; there is no roster, membership operation, group identifier or credential issuance. Signal's private-group system (encrypted roster, master key, GroupChange authentication, zk credential issuance) lives in the separate AGPL storage-service (Bigtable) and in the Signal app code, not in libsignal or Signal-Server. Option B therefore means writing a prekey directory, a per-device queue, a group-state store with credential issuance, the client group-change state machine, device linking and a Tor transport (libsignal-net targets the Signal service). The closing list at :393 concedes most of this, but the layer table reads as reuse. Separately: libsignal identity keys are Curve25519 (type byte 0x05, XEdDSA signatures) and in Signal's deployed model are per account, shared by all linked devices; (device ID, H(identity key)) therefore does not identify a device, and "remove a device" cannot be expressed as rejecting an identity key. Per-device identity keys are possible in a bespoke Option B but depart from the Sesame model the design cites. Finally, the Bodferd layer is Go, libsignal has Java/Swift/TypeScript bindings only, and bespoke FFI is forbidden, so the "narrow adapter" is either FFI, an IPC boundary with a bespoke control protocol, or a second implementation of the verifier in another language, which the v1 sections warn against. The server-cost sentence (:341) names FoundationDB and omits DynamoDB, four Redis clusters, object storage, APNs/FCM, registration service, CDSI, SVR and the separate groups backend.

Evidence: docs/design.md:339, :341, :357-363, :365, :369, :379, :393; upstream: signalapp/libsignal rust/protocol/src/group_cipher.rs, sender_keys.rs, rust/core/src/curve.rs; signalapp/storage-service GroupsController; signalapp/Signal-Server service/config/sample.yml.

Remediation: Re-title Option B as "a new messenger reusing libsignal's pairwise ratchet"; state the per-account identity key consequence and choose per-device or per-account binding; replace the Go/no-FFI sentence with the actual consequence (a non-Go client).

A11 — High: the stock-Signal companion option cannot meet the design's own gates, and should be concluded rather than piloted#
